item.title: Ginkakuji, the Silver Pavilion: Restraint and Raked Sand — Guide
item.description: Ginkakuji, the Silver Pavilion, is the quieter, more contemplative counterpart to the golden Kinkakuji across the city. Built in 1482 as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa and converted to a Zen temple on his death, it was never actually clad in silver — its beauty lies instead in restraint. The dark wooden pavilion overlooks a refined garden of moss, a still pond and, most famously, a great cone of raked white sand and a silvery ‘sea’ meant to reflect the moon.

item.title: Keage Incline: The Cherry-Blossom Railway Slope — Guide
item.description: The Keage Incline is a short stretch of disused railway slope near Nanzenji, built as part of the ingenious Lake Biwa Canal that once carried boats between the lake and Kyoto by hauling them up and down this ramp on rail cradles. Long out of use, its rusting twin tracks have become one of the city’s loveliest walks: some ninety cherry trees line the slope, and in early April they arch overhead into a tunnel of blossom above the old rails, drawing photographers and strollers.

item.title: Maruyama Park: Kyoto's Favourite Cherry-Blossom Park — Guide
item.description: Maruyama Park, tucked behind Yasaka Shrine at the foot of the Higashiyama hills, is the most popular public park in Kyoto and its most famous spot for hanami. Laid out in the Meiji era, it is a gentle landscape of ponds, streams, stone lanterns and winding paths, with tea houses and restaurants around its edges. At its heart stands a huge shidarezakura, a weeping cherry tree, which in early April is floodlit after dark and surrounded by revellers and food stalls in one of the city’s great cherry-blossom scenes.

item.title: Sanjusangendo: The Hall of 1,001 Kannon — Guide
item.description: Sanjusangendo is one of Kyoto’s most quietly overwhelming sights: a long, narrow wooden hall, at 120 metres the longest in Japan, filled with a thousand and one statues of Kannon, the Buddhist deity of compassion. Rank upon rank of gilded, thousand-armed figures stand in tiered rows to either side of a great seated central Kannon, each face subtly different, backed by twenty-eight guardian deities and the thunder and wind gods carved with astonishing dynamism.

item.title: Higashiyama Hanatouro Guide: The Lantern Festival & What Replaced It
item.description: Important update: The Higashiyama Hanatouro festival has ended. Its final edition was held in March 2022, and the organisers concluded the event after roughly two decades. If you came looking for it, this guide explains what it was, why it stopped — and, more usefully, the beautiful evening illuminations and night temple visits you can still enjoy in Higashiyama today. For about twenty years, the Higashiyama Hanatouro (“flower and light path”) transformed eastern Kyoto into a magical evening promenade each March, lining the historic stone streets between Kiyomizu-dera and Maruyama Park with thousands of lanterns and seasonal flower displays.

item.title: Kiyomizu-dera Guide: The Temple on Stilts Above Kyoto
item.description: Perched on the wooded slopes of Higashiyama, Kiyomizu-dera juts out over the hillside on a vast wooden stage held up by enormous pillars — built, famously, without a single nail. From the stage you look out over a sea of maple and cherry trees to the rooftops of Kyoto beyond. It is one of Japan’s most beloved temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the climax of the most atmospheric temple approach in the city: the stone-paved, shop-lined slopes of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka.

item.title: Kyoto Kimono Rental Guide: Dressing the Part in the Old Capital
item.description: There is no more atmospheric way to explore Kyoto’s historic streets than dressed in a kimono. As you walk the stone lanes of Higashiyama or cross a bridge in Arashiyama, the traditional silhouette transforms the experience — and the photographs. Kimono rental in Kyoto is easy, affordable, and hugely popular with visitors of every nationality and gender: shops dress you head to toe, style your hair, and send you out for the day.

item.title: Philosopher's Path Guide: Kyoto's Most Beautiful Walk
item.description: The Philosopher’s Path (Tetsugaku-no-michi) is a stone-paved walking trail that follows a cherry-tree-lined canal through the quiet temple district of eastern Kyoto. Named for a famous philosophy professor who walked it daily in meditation on his way to Kyoto University, it strings together some of the city’s loveliest temples, shrines, cafés, and craft shops over about two gentle kilometres. In cherry-blossom season it becomes a tunnel of pink reflected in the water; in autumn, a corridor of red and gold.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Fukushima: Aizu, Higashiyama & Bandai
item.description: Fukushima Prefecture — the largest in Tohoku — is slowly reclaiming its place as one of Japan’s great travel destinations. The areas described in this guide (Aizu-Wakamatsu, Higashiyama, and the Bandai-Asahi plateau) are geographically and culturally remote from the 2011 coastal zone and have been open to tourism throughout. The prefecture rewards independent travellers seeking samurai history, excellent onsen, and spectacular mountain scenery without crowds. Best Areas to Stay Aizu-Wakamatsu — Samurai Castle Town The most complete surviving castle-town atmosphere in Tohoku.
